message.content:
You are doing part of a literature novelty check for a planned preregistered study. Return findings as your final message (no report files).

PLANNED STUDY (context): Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset (Röseler et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; 412 anchoring items, 96 studies), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = (central estimate under high anchor − central estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor); Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995) changes with anchor extremity (anchor distance relative to true value and/or to uncertainty about the quantity), at the item level, and compare against predictions simulated from four process models: resource-rational adjustment (Lieder et al. 2018 PBR), anchor integration model (Turner & Schley 2016 Cogn Psychol), insufficient adjustment (Epley & Gilovich 2006), selective accessibility / plausibility (Mussweiler & Strack; Wegener et al. 2001).

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- Do NOT download or open any data file (csv, xlsx, rds, zip of data) from osf.io/ygnvb or any OSF data component, or any supplementary dataset. Papers (PDF/HTML text) only. This is a blinding rule.
- Write scratch files only as /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_sw_* (unique prefix; other agents share that dir).
- Every number you report needs its source location (page, table, or section) in the text you read. Mark anything you only saw in an abstract as "abstract only" and anything not read as UNVERIFIED. Never fabricate DOIs; verify DOIs via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>.
- OpenAlex: `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`, then append `&api_key=<key>`; the default key is out of quota today, rotate through the comma-separated $OPENALEX_API_KEYS (a helper exists: `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py search "<query>" "&filter=publication_year:2022-2026"` and `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py cites <OpenAlexWorkID>`). Semantic Scholar API needs no key. Skills available: download-paper (download PDFs by DOI), check-claim. For PsyArXiv PDFs try the OSF API: https://api.osf.io/v2/preprints/<id>/?embed=primary_file then the file's download link (preprint PDFs are fine to download; data files are not).

TASKS:
A. Schley & Weingarten anchoring meta-analysis. Crossref shows: 10.31234/osf.io/teq7k (2023) and teq7k_v2 (2025-12) "50 Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis"; SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.4605057, 10.2139/ssrn.5893864, 10.2139/ssrn.5114456 ("50 Years of Anchoring: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects"); and reportedly Management Science doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238. Verify the MnSc DOI via Crossref (title, authors, year, volume/issue). Establish whether these are one paper or two. Read the FULL TEXT of the latest available version (prefer teq7k_v2 or the MnSc version). Extract precisely: (1) data sources (did they use OpAQ? how many effects/studies/items), (2) whether and how they coded anchor extremity/distance (definition: relative to true value? to uncertainty/SD? percentiles?), (3) at what level (effect/item/study) extremity moderation was tested and the exact numeric result, including any nonlinearity (inverted U?), (4) which effect-size metric(s) they used — Hedges g only, or any proportional/unitless adjustment metric such as the anchoring index, (5) which theories they contrasted and how (e.g., "meta-study", theory-driven predictions, model fitting?), (6) results for random/uninformative anchors. Quote key sentences with page numbers.
B. Young, Speekenbrink, Buyukyildirim, Chung et al. 2026, "Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in item-based anchoring", Cognitive Psychology, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796. Read (full text if accessible, else abstract + any preprint). What did they do; did they use OpAQ data; did they fit computational models; any analysis of anchor extremity or proportional adjustment?
C. Search 2022–2026 for computational/process-model papers on numerical anchoring: queries like "anchoring computational model", "anchoring Bayesian model", "anchoring resource-rational", "anchoring sampling model estimation", "anchoring adjustment model fitting", "anchor extremity anchoring index", "anchoring index anchor distance", "anchor plausibility extremity nonmonotonic". Use OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and WebSearch/Google Scholar-style searches (load WebSearch/WebFetch via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). Also check who cites Lieder et al. 2018 (10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 and 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6) and Turner & Schley 2016 (10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) in 2022–2026 and flag any that fit models to multi-study/multi-item anchoring data or relate proportional adjustment to anchor extremity. For each relevant hit: citation, verified DOI, one-paragraph summary of design/measure/key numbers, and how close it is to the planned study (0–3).
D. Briefly: what exactly did Lieder et al. 2018 (both PBR papers) and Turner & Schley 2016 fit their models to (which datasets, how many items, which measures), and did either derive/test a prediction about how the anchoring index varies with anchor extremity? Give numbers (e.g., Lieder's simulated vs observed AI for Jacowitz & Kahneman items; any anchor-extremity simulations such as Russo & Schoemaker or Chapman & Johnson-type data). Page references.

Final message: structured findings per task A–D, with verified DOIs, page-referenced numbers, and a closeness rating to the planned study.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.

  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a

  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),

`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items

   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.

   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.

   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

```html
<link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🦸</text></svg>">
```

  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.

  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

# Working with APIs

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

- **A word starting with `=` triggers command-path expansion.** `echo ===` fails with
  `== not found` and aborts the rest of the compound command. Use `echo "---"` or
  quote it.
- **An unmatched glob is fatal, not literal.** `ls foo*`, `git branch --list bak*`,
  and `grep --include=*.html` abort with `no matches found` when nothing matches.
  Quote globs passed as arguments (`--include='*.html'`); guard optional ones
  (`ls foo* 2>/dev/null || true`).

## Chrome Extension: Local Files, Tabs, Busy Pages

- The extension cannot open `file://` URLs. To view local HTML, serve the directory
  (`python3 -m http.server <port>`, backgrounded) and open
  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.
- If a screenshot/scroll/javascript call times out, the page is mid-load: take one
  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

For any Google Workspace task (Docs, Sheets, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slides, Forms), use the `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`). Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

Never pipe `gws` output directly into a JSON parser: keyring warnings and preamble
contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

Every standalone HTML file gets an emoji favicon as a `data:` URI, right after `<title>`:

```html

```

- Pick for the page's **topic**, never its type (no 📋 for every plan, 📊 for every
  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
- Safari ignores SVG favicons: for participant- or reviewer-facing pages use
  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

To open a webpage for the user, use the Bash tool to run `open <url>`. Do not use Claude artefacts by default. Keep scratch files local, deploy single collaborative files to surge.sh, and use GH pages for project-related files that are supposed to be shared.

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them.

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. One of the most robust phenomena studied across the social behavioral sciences is numeric anchoring, in which a comparison against a presumed-to-be arbitrary number preceding a judgment can influence a myriad of real-world-relevant judgments. The authors meta-analyze the expansive literature containing 2,601 total effect sizes (1,280 comparing high anchors against low anchors), finding a large (Hedges’ g  = 0.825, 95% CI[0.765, 0.884], I2 = 93.73%) effect that remains large even after accounting for extensive publication bias. Evi?dence suggests reduced (or null) effects associated with incidental anchoring (i.e., numeric priming), anchors from different dimensions, or from random numbers, the presence of incentives or debiasing interventions, and whether the anchor provides directional information. The authors provide a comprehensive review of both the empirical and theoretical landscape, and offer recommendations for consolidating the literature, improving theory testing, future development of theory and methods related to anchoring, and guidance for managers attempting to use anchoring effects in strategic and policy decisions.

1	          50 Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical
2	               Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis
3	                                                    Dan R. Schley
4	                           Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, [email redacted]
5	
6	                                                   Evan Weingarten
7	                      Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, [email redacted]
8	
9	
10	     One of the most robust phenomena studied across the social behavioral sciences is numeric anchoring, in
11	
12	     which a comparison against a presumed-to-be arbitrary number preceding a judgment can influence a myriad
13	
14	     of real-world-relevant judgments. The authors meta-analyze the expansive literature containing 2,601 total
15	
16	     effect sizes (1,280 comparing high anchors against low anchors), finding a large (Hedges’g = 0.825, 95% CI
17	
18	     [0.765, 0.884], I 2 = 93.73%) effect that remains large even after accounting for extensive publication bias. Evi-
19	
20	     dence suggests reduced (or null) effects associated with incidental anchoring (i.e., numeric priming), anchors
21	
22	     from different dimensions, or from random numbers, the presence of incentives or debiasing interventions,
23	
24	     and whether the anchor provides directional information. The authors provide a comprehensive review of
25	
26	     both the empirical and theoretical landscape, and offer recommendations for consolidating the literature,
27	
28	     improving theory testing, future development of theory and methods related to anchoring, and guidance for
29	
30	     managers attempting to use anchoring effects in strategic and policy decisions.
31	
32	     Key words : Anchoring, Judgment and Decision Making, Meta-Analysis
33	
34	
35	
36	
37	1.     Introduction
38	Every day, people make numeric judgments such as estimating commute times, bidding on used
39	
40	cars, or predicting restaurant wait times. Although such judgments could rely on deliberate mem-
41	
42	ory search and weighted cue integration, decades of research suggest otherwise. Instead, peo-
43	
44	ple routinely assimilate their estimates toward salient numbers in the environment. This phe-
45	
46	nomenon—known as the anchoring effect—was popularized by Tversky and Kahneman (1974),
47	
48	who showed that even an irrelevant random number from a rigged “wheel of fortune” (10 or 65)
49	
50	biased participants’ estimates of African nations in the U.N.: those who saw 65 gave higher esti-
51	
52	mates than those who saw 10.
53	
54	                                                             1
55	   This basic paradigm—exposure to a (sometimes meaningless) number followed by an assimilated
56	
57	judgment—has become a foundational demonstration of bias in human judgment. However, over
58	
59	the past five decades, this paradigm has splintered into a wide array of methods, each adapting
60	
61	the original logic in distinct ways. What counts as “anchoring” now spans a remarkably broad set
62	
63	of contexts, mechanisms, and domains.
64	
65	  In some studies, anchors are subliminal —numbers flashed too quickly to be consciously rec-
66	
67	ognized but are argued to influence willingness-to-pay (Mussweiler and Englich 2005). In others,
68	
69	anchors are merely part of the background: people exposed to a restaurant named “Studio 97”
70	
71	give higher price estimates than those exposed to “Studio 17” (Critcher and Gilovich 2008). Some
72	
73	studies embed anchors directly in task framing, such as stating that Chicago’s population is below
74	
75	five million before asking for an estimate (Simmons et al. 2010), or providing a list price before
76	
77	home appraisal (Northcraft and Neale 1987). Others prompt participants to explicitly evaluate the
78	
79	accuracy of the anchor (e.g., “Is the Mississippi River longer than 1,200 miles?”).
80	
81	  Studies also differ in the plausibility of the anchor (e.g., age of Gandhi at death greater than 271
82	
83	years; Mussweiler and Strack 2001, Wegener et al. 2001), or whether it shares the same dimension as
84	
85	the estimate (e.g., grams of fat vs. number of calories; Frederick and Mochon 2012). Some anchors
86	
87	are transparently irrelevant (Tversky and Kahneman 1974); others are labeled as uninformative
88	
89	(Simmons et al. 2010); and some, like sentencing requests from prosecutors, may convey diagnostic
90	
91	information such as precedents, laws, or norms (Bystranowski et al. 2021).
92	
93	  Who provides the anchor also varies. Some are introduced by the experimenter. Others are self-
94	
95	generated — participants might consider “1776” as a starting date when estimating when George
96	
97	Washington became president (Epley and Gilovich 2001, 2006). Still others are externally cued
98	
99	from one’s own memory, such as writing down the last two digits of one’s Social Security number
100	
101	before estimating a product’s price (Ariely et al. 2003).
102	
103	  Judgment contexts vary widely, as do participants. Beyond classic trivia tasks with students
104	
105	(Jacowitz and Kahneman 1995, Strack and Mussweiler 1997), anchoring has been studied with
106	                                          2
107	 appraisers pricing homes (Northcraft and Neale 1987), consumers evaluating goods (Ariely et al.
108	
109	2003, Simonson and Drolet 2004), negotiators setting offers (Galinsky and Mussweiler 2001,
110	
111	Loschelder et al. 2014), and judges assigning sentences (Englich 2008, Glöckner and Englich 2015).
112	
113	     Despite this diversity, two elements define what studies tend to label themselves as “anchoring”.
114	
115	First, a numeric value precedes the judgment—whether from an experimenter, the participant, or
116	
117	the environment. Second, the resulting estimate shifts toward that number. Still, the conceptual
118	
119	sprawl has made it difficult to define anchoring in practice. Today’s typical anchoring study often
120	
121	looks little like the original. And the extremes—subliminal cues, self-generated anchors, or ecolog-
122	
123	ically valid price signals—make clear that anchoring need not reflect a single process but a family
124	
125	of related phenomena.
126	
127	     This manuscript re-integrates this fragmented literature. We begin by reviewing seven major
128	
129	theories of anchoring. We then propose a framework for organizing the wide variety of paradigms
130	
131	and moderators. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis and offer recommendations for
132	
133	future research. Our mapping of this landscape reveals when and why judgments are pulled toward
134	
135	numeric cues—and how a seemingly simple bias reflects a surprisingly complex set of processes.
136	
137	1.1.      A Brief Review of Existing Theories
138	
139	The anchoring effect has accumulated at least seven different theories proposing underlying mech-
140	
141	anisms that drive anchoring effects. While there are a number of theoretical accounts that could be
142	
143	applied to anchoring (e.g., Schwarz 1994), we focus on those that self-identify as distinct theories
144	
145	of anchoring effects.1
146	
147	     1.1.1.    Anchoring-and-Adjustment. The core proposition of the original Anchoring-and-
148	
149	Adjustment theory is that when attending to an anchor stimulus, decision-makers begin with that
150	
151	anchor and adjust away from that value (Tversky and Kahneman 1974). For example, in the
152	
153	1
154	    Schwarz (1994) did not directly discuss anchoring, but conversational inferences in judgments and decisions more
155	
156	broadly. The notion that anchoring may be due to conversational inferences was popularized by Jacowitz and Kah-
157	
158	neman (1995) and has since been referenced within the literature.
159	                                                          3
160	 context of judging percentage of African countries in the United Nations, people start at the 10%
161	
162	anchor then iteratively adjust the estimate upward, stopping periodically (e.g., at 20%) to evaluate
163	
164	whether that interim value is within the realm of plausible values.
165	
166	  The adjustment process ends via one of two mechanisms. The first mechanism supposes that
167	
168	adjustment is effortful, and decision-makers do not exert effort to adjust all the way back to the
169	
170	true value (Epley and Gilovich 2001, 2006). For example, a decision-maker may adjust up to 20%
171	
172	then reconsider whether this value is an appropriate guess about the percentage of African nations
173	
174	in the U.N. If the estimate is still too low, they repeat this process. Because this process is effortful,
175	
176	decision-makers may stop this adjustment prematurely with an estimate still assimilated toward
177	
178	the anchor.
179	
180	  The second mechanism asserts that decision-makers have some knowledge about the true value
181	
182	for the judgment and this knowledge is implied by a range of plausible values (Quattrone et al.
183	
184	1984). When anchors are outside of that plausible range, decision-makers adjust until they reach
185	
186	the boundaries of that plausible range. Because the decision-maker stops at the first value within
187	
188	this range, that first value is more likely to be closer to the starting anchor stimulus than to the
189	
190	middle of the range.
191	
192	  1.1.2.   Numeric Priming. Numeric Priming contends that any stimulus activated in the
193	
194	environment can be encoded into short-term memory, and the activation of that stimulus can influ-
195	
196	ence subsequent judgments (Wilson et al. 1996, Critcher and Gilovich 2008, Reitsma-van Rooijen
197	
198	and Daamen 2006). As such, numbers encountered in the decision environment, whether they are
199	
200	directly attended to via a comparison or indirectly as background features of the environment,
201	
202	become accessible in short-term memory and are then conflated when evaluating a target stimulus.
203	
204	  1.1.3.   Selective Accessibility Hypothesis. The Selective Accessibility Hypothesis suggests
205	
206	that when presented with an anchoring question (e.g., “Is the Mississippi River greater than or
207	
208	less than 1,500 miles”), the decision-maker performs a confirmatory hypothesis test about the
209	
210	possibility that the anchor is equal to the true value (Strack and Mussweiler 1997, Mussweiler and
211	                                                   4
212	 Strack 1999, Chapman and Johnson 1999). When engaging in any confirmatory search, decision-
213	
214	makers selectively search for information that is consistent with the query (Klayman and Ha 1987).
215	
216	Because this anchor-consistent knowledge is now in short-term memory due to this confirmatory
217	
218	search, that anchor-consistent knowledge biases judgments in the direction of the anchor value.2
219	
220	     1.1.4.    Attitudinal Perspective. The Attitudinal Perspective applies the tenets of the elab-
221	
222	oration likelihood model to the anchoring effect (Petty and Cacioppo 1986, Wegener et al. 2010).
223	
224	This theory contends that decision-makers can engage with anchors via a more deliberative central-
225	
226	route process whereby they engage in a process somewhat analogous to the Selective Accessibility
227	
228	Hypothesis (i.e., confirmatory reasoning about why the anchor is related to the true value). Alter-
229	
230	natively, decision-makers can process anchors via a less deliberative, peripheral-route process in
231	
232	which the stimulus acts as a prime analogous to the process described in the Numeric Priming
233	
234	account. Additionally, this is the only account that explicitly argues that anchors can serve as
235	
236	contextually diagnostic cues (Schwarz 1994).
237	
238	     1.1.5.    Scale Distortion Theory of Anchoring. Rather than anchors changing decision-
239	
240	makers’ perception of a focal stimulus, the Scale Distortion account suggests that anchors affect
241	
242	the internal scale decision-makers use to map their knowledge onto a numeric response (Frederick
243	
244	and Mochon 2012, Mochon and Frederick 2013). Scale Distortion argues that anchoring occurs not
245	
246	by changing the decision-maker’s belief about the ordinal rank of the target (e.g., a low anchor
247	
248	about the length of the Mississippi River should not make decision-makers think of the river as
249	
250	shorter relative to other rivers) but via a shift in the scale by which they express their belief (i.e.,
251	
252	a low anchor pulls down the numbers decision-makers use to express the length of all rivers).
253	
254	     1.1.6.    Extremeness Aversion. According to Extremeness Aversion (Lewis et al. 2019), as
255	
256	in Anchoring-and-Adjustment, decision-makers begin at a presented anchor value and adjust away
257	
258	from the anchor. The authors propose an additional stopping mechanism to the two specified above:
259	2
260	    We coalesce the Strack and Mussweiler (1997) and Chapman and Johnson (1999) here because there is considerable
261	
262	overlap but acknowledge that there are important theoretical differences.
263	                                                         5
264	 decision-makers stop adjusting when they feel that their adjustment from the anchor is too extreme
265	
266	(i.e., far away from the anchor).
267	
268	  1.1.7.   Noise Theory. The Noise Theory is centrally focused on the plausible range of values
269	
270	decision-makers evaluate when responding to an anchor (Lee and Morewedge 2022). The amount
271	
272	of noise in a decision-maker’s representation maps onto how wide that range is. For a given anchor,
273	
274	any increase in noise in the representation will increase the anchoring effect. For example, higher
275	
276	magnitudes have greater noise, which translates into larger anchoring effects. Further, those with
277	
278	higher knowledge have less noisy representations, which reduces anchoring effects.
279	
280	2.   Theory-Based and Exploratory Moderators
281	The above section suggests that different paradigms and contexts were used to study different
282	
283	theories. For example, studies testing the Anchoring-and-Adjustment perspective involved quite
284	
285	different moderators than studies testing numeric priming (e.g., incentives versus mood). As such,
286	
287	the collection of moderators across the whole literature appears disjointed. In this section, we
288	
289	propose a framework for categorizing the different design features across this wide literature. While
290	
291	some moderators within the literature pertain to specific cognitive processes (e.g., selective retrieval
292	
293	of anchor-consistent knowledge from memory), other moderators are not rooted in theoretical
294	
295	processes but are intended to be phenomenological (e.g., robustness of anchoring to the presence
296	
297	of incentives).
298	
299	  We categorize the different mechanisms from existing theories into four general components that
300	
301	broadly encompass the moderator space: Salience, Inference Making, Memory Retrieval, and Depth
302	
303	of Information Processing. Note, Salience and Depth of Information Processing are not processes in
304	
305	and of themselves, but act to change the amount (e.g., extent of elaboration) or type of information
306	
307	being processed (e.g., attention to the anchor stimulus relative to other features in the decision
308	
309	environment). An overview of these four components, which moderators pertain to each, and which
310	
311	theories make predictions of which moderators is provided in Table 1. We adopt a conservative
312	
313	coding approach such that the predictions shown reflect only what each theory explicitly states, or
314	
315	is given with minimal inference (i.e., the theory necessitates a prediction), rather than what could
316	
317	be implied or interpreted from its underlying mechanisms.
318	                                                6
319	                            Table 1        Categories of Anchoring Moderators and Corresponding Theories
320	                                                                                      Anchoring Theories
321	                                        Anchoring-and     Numeric      Selective       Attitudinal       Scale         Extremeness     Noise    Effect

354	  further extremity no longer increases the size of the effect.
355	
356	
357	
358	
359	  2.1.      Salience
360	
361	  One common feature of existing theories is the role of perceptual salience of the anchor in the
362	
363	  judgment.3 For example, Numeric Priming (Wilson et al. 1996) and the Attitudinal Perspective
364	
365	  (Wegener et al. 2010) suppose that attending, albeit incidentally, to anchors results in the anchor
366	
367	  being active in working memory at the moment of the focal judgment. Anchoring-and-Adjustment
368	
369	  (e.g., Quattrone et al. 1984) and Extremeness Aversion (Lewis et al. 2019) require attention to the
370	
371	  anchor value for adjustment to begin. That is, the adjustment process is effortful, so it requires
372	
373	  deliberate attention to the anchor as a starting point. Moreover, the Selective Accessibility Hypoth-
374	
375	  esis (e.g., Strack and Mussweiler 1997) requires the anchor to be attended to for there to be a
376	
377	  confirmatory-hypothesis-testing process. Thus, the existing theories provide some consensus that
378	
379	  anchoring effects must operate, in part, via attentional processes and features that alter attention
380	
381	  (or the amount of information derived when attended to) should influence anchoring effects.
382	
383	  3
384	      This is intended to be a broad category label to capture a range of related perceptual processes at play in anchoring
385	
386	  judgments. For example, any features that alter the visual salience of the stimulus or the ease with which decision-
387	
388	  makers can, or want to, attend to the anchor would fall within this category.
389	                                                                            7
390	      Primed/Incidental Anchors. Incidental/Primed anchors are anchors with no explicit relationship
391	
392	to the target judgment. For example, whether a restaurant is named Studio 17 or Studio 97 should
393	
394	not be diagnostic of its meal price. The Numeric Priming account supposes that increased exposure
395	
396	increases anchoring from these incidental anchors (Wilson et al. 1996). Anchoring-and-Adjustment
397	
398	contends that no anchoring is possible here, as there is no explicit anchor from which to adjust.
399	
400	Scale Distortion has contended this form of anchoring is not robust as it does not change the scale
401	
402	(Mochon and Frederick 2013).4 The Attitudinal Perspective argues explicitly that anchoring can
403	
404	occur with primed anchors via the peripheral route, but does not differentiate whether those effects
405	
406	would be larger, smaller, or similar in magnitude (Wegener et al. 2010).
407	
408	     Temporal Delay. A temporal delay between the anchor and focal judgment may reduce the acces-
409	
410	sibility of an anchor in memory and thus its salience. Selective Accessibility predicts anchoring
411	
412	persists and the effect is durable (i.e., no attenuation) after delay (Mussweiler 2001). The Attitu-
413	
414	dinal Perspective predicts anchoring persists with delays, but may be slightly weaker depending
415	
416	on depth of processing (Blankenship et al. 2008).
417	
418	2.2.      Inference Making
419	
420	Decision-makers must process not only the focal stimulus, but the implied context by which a
421	
422	stimulus is presented. This role of inference-making goes back to when, originally, Tversky and
423	
424	Kahneman (1974) used a spinning wheel to block inferences that the anchor is informative. Only the
425	
426	Attitudinal Perspective explicitly discusses the role of inference-making as a feature of its theory
427	
428	(Wegener et al. 2010). The moderators in this section can be thought to influence the perceived
429	
430	informativeness of the anchor such that the context of the anchor signals whether decision-makers
431	
432	should or should not use the anchor value (Grice 1975).
433	4
434	    The Selective Accessibility Hypothesis makes conflicting predictions. On one hand, Strack and Mussweiler (1997)
435	
436	argues that anchoring won’t occur when the anchor and target concern different judgments (e.g., width vs. height of
437	
438	Brandenburg gate), implying that seeing a number that’s not directly relevant to the confirmatory-hypothesis-test
439	
440	mechanisms is insufficient for anchoring. But, Mussweiler and Englich (2005) argued that selective accessibility can
441	
442	occur with primed anchors. Note, Selective Accessibility does not predict whether primed anchors produce a larger
443	
444	or smaller effect.
445	                                                          8
446	     Comparison Question. Despite the original experimental setup attempting to present an unin-
447	
448	formative anchor (e.g., spinning wheel of fortune Tversky and Kahneman 1974), some have argued
449	
450	that conversational norms are still inferred by decision makers (Grice 1975, Schwarz 1994, Wegener
451	
452	et al. 2010). Directing attention to a random number and having participants compare that num-
453	
454	ber with the target judgment (e.g., is [TARGET] greater than or less than [ANCHOR]?) might
455	
456	signal that the number is in fact meaningful. If not conversational inferences directly, others have
457	
458	argued that these comparison questions can differentially activate information consistent with the
459	
460	anchor’s value (Chapman and Johnson 1999, Strack and Mussweiler 1997). Numeric Priming is the
461	
462	only account to explicitly make a prediction about this moderator (Wilson et al. 1996, Study 2).
463

641

779	2.6.   The Present Investigation.
780	
781	We report a meta-analysis of the anchoring literature. We concentrate on comparing high against
782	
783	low anchors across 1,280 effect sizes in 482 studies in a primary database, and analyze additional
784	
785	forms of anchoring in the online appendices.
786	
787	  This meta-analysis builds on several smaller related meta-analyses. Anchoring is one of the most
788	
789	prototypical biases in the judgment-and-decision-making, behavioral-economics, and other related
790	
791	literatures, but has yet to receive as comprehensive a treatment as in the present manuscript.
792	
793	There are a couple meta-analyses exploring anchoring within Law (Bystranowski et al. 2021) and
794	
795	Economics (Li et al. 2021), each impressive in their own right. Both were indicative of smaller
796	
797	effects of non-diagnostic anchors from different dimensions, with Li et al. (2021) finding reduced
798	
799	effects associated with incentives and transparently random anchors.

1711	5.   General Discussion
1712	Anchoring research ranges from trivial knowledge tasks to high-stakes decisions, yet no single theory
1713	
1714	explains every form of assimilation. We define anchoring broadly as any case where a decision-maker
1715	
1716	encounters a prior number—whether experimenter-provided, incidental, or self-generated—and
1717	
1718	then shifts their estimate toward it. This broad definition exposes both anchoring’s ubiquity and
1719	                                                32
1720	 its theoretical challenges. Surface differences like estimating river lengths versus responding to sen-
1721	
1722	tencing demands, or explicit comparative questions versus incidental number exposure—mask a
1723	
1724	shared outcome- assimilation toward a numeric cue. Such methodological diversity suggests anchor-
1725	
1726	ing comprises a family of processes—selective retrieval of anchor-consistent information, iterative
1727	
1728	adjustment from the starting point, internal scale distortion, and more—each dominant under par-
1729	
1730	ticular conditions. Instead of forcing a single mechanism, we propose treating anchoring as a class
1731	
1732	of effects with a common input (a prior number) and output (a biased estimate), acknowledging
1733	
1734	multiple underlying paths.
1735	
1736	5.1.   Evaluating Existing Theories
1737	
1738	In Table 1 in the introduction, we outlined the predictions for each of the seven existing theories
1739	
1740	within the anchoring literature. Most theories do not make explicit predictions for all of the moder-
1741	
1742	ators in the literature. When we attempted to link theories to each moderator, this was not feasible
1743	
1744	without extensive conjecture about how each theory’s mechanisms operate for each moderator. For
1745	
1746	example, cognitive load may increase anchoring for Numeric Priming if it reduces the accessibility
1747	
1748	of other inputs (Reitsma-van Rooijen and Daamen 2006), but it may also decrease anchoring if
1749	
1750	it limits attention to the anchor (Wilson et al. 1996). Instead of counting up winners and losers,
1751	
1752	we instead take a broader reflection on each theory and evaluate two key questions: 1) whether
1753	
1754	the general mechanisms (rather than specific moderator predictions) find empirical support, and
1755	
1756	2) whether there are issues in the theory that prevent its use for prediction.
1757	
1758	  Anchoring-and-Adjustment posits that judgments begin at the anchor and proceed via an
1759	
1760	effortful adjustment (Tversky and Kahneman 1974). Crucially, adjustment cannot commence unless
1761	
1762	the anchor is explicitly attended to, so manipulations that diminish anchor salience such as inciden-
1763	
1764	tal or subliminal primes, removal of a direct comparison prompt, or anchors drawn from unrelated
1765	
1766	stimuli, should weaken the effect. Our meta-analysis confirms substantial reductions in anchoring
1767	
1768	under some of these conditions (i.e., incidental anchors and incidental stimuli). Yet, a core feature
1769	
1770	of the theory, whether adjustment unfolds in multiple small steps or a single coarse shift, remains
1771	                                              33
1772	 untested.14 Similarly, the theory is correct that accuracy incentives reduce anchoring. However,
1773	
1774	there is less clarity about the mechanisms underlying this result, which could reflect greater effortful
1775	
1776	adjustment or, alternatively, enhanced retrieval of decision-relevant information. Finally, contrary
1777	
1778	to predictions, anchor precision did not reliably moderate the effect.
1779	
1780	     Numeric Priming proposes that incidental exposure to numbers can influence subsequent
1781	
1782	judgments (Wilson et al. 1996). Given the very weak evidence for priming effects in the current
1783	
1784	meta-analysis, as well as in psychology more broadly (Mac Giolla et al. 2024), we encourage scholars
1785	
1786	to investigate more crucial features of the anchoring puzzle. For example, Wilson et al. (1996)
1787	
1788	argued that attention to numbers in the environment was a driver of anchoring (i.e., larger effects
1789	
1790	when the anchor is presented via an explicit comparative question versus incidental exposure).
1791	
1792	Rather than investigating whether anchoring can occur in low-elaboration contexts, it is more
1793	
1794	critical to understand exactly how much attention is required for it to occur and the functional
1795	
1796	relationship between amount of attention or information processing and size of the effect.
1797	
1798	     The Selective Accessibility Hypothesis combines two processes: a confirmatory search that
1799	
1800	selectively retrieves anchor-consistent information (Mussweiler and Strack 1999) and evaluation
1801	
1802	of the anchor against one’s prior plausible range (Mussweiler and Strack 2001). Like Anchoring-
1803	
1804	and-Adjustment, it requires that the anchor appear decision-relevant (i.e., on the same dimension
1805	
1806	or stimulus, even if explicitly stated to be random Strack and Mussweiler 1997). But, an explicit
1807	
1808	confirmatory-hypothesis test assumes decision-makers elaborate deeply. This elaboration is at odds
1809	
1810	with Mussweiler and Englich (2005), who simultaneously argued that subliminal primes can acti-
1811	
1812	vate anchor-consistent knowledge. We suggest that Chapman and Johnson (1999)’s less restrictive
1813	
1814	“activation” account may be more appropriate as a mechanism as it does not necessitate an explicit
1815	
1816	hypothesis test. The second, and more substantial, issue for this account is that there is limited
1817	
1818	direct evidence of anchor-consistent knowledge, and Harris et al. (2019) recently failed to replicate
1819	
1820	mechanistic evidence for anchor-consistent knowledge in memory.
1821	14
1822	     Epley and Gilovich (2001) captured verbal protocols but did not distinguish iterative (i.e., number of steps) from
1823	
1824	a single one-step adjustment.
1825	                                                           34
1826	   The Attitudinal Perspective is built on top of the mature attitudes-and-persuasion literature
1827	
1828	(Wegener et al. 2010). Although this framework is conceptually rich, there is a critical gap: it
1829	
1830	does not specify whether deeper elaboration amplifies anchoring by focusing on the anchor itself
1831	
1832	or attenuates it by eliciting counter-arguments. Our attempts to map attitudinal predictions onto
1833	
1834	numeric anchors (Table 1) revealed many conflicting expectations. To be testable, this account
1835	
1836	must define how elaboration (1) modulates attention to anchor information, (2) triggers retrieval
1837	
1838	of anchor-inconsistent information, and (3) integrates these streams into the final judgment.
1839	
1840	  Scale Distortion conceptualizes anchoring as a shift in an internal response scale (Frederick
1841	
1842	and Mochon 2012). Similar to Anchoring-and-Adjustment, it correctly predicts that the relevance
1843	
1844	of the anchor, particularly with regard to the alignment of stimulus and dimension is related to
1845	
1846	anchoring. Yet its binary predictions (i.e., anchoring occurs only with identical units) overlooks the
1847	
1848	potential of related scales/dimensions. For example, a tree-height anchor may not bias estimates
1849	
1850	of numbers of trees in a forest but could influence tree age judgments, since tree height and age
1851	
1852	correlate. Advancing the theory requires formalizing a dimensional-similarity metric and mapping
1853	
1854	partial overlaps onto proportional shifts in anchoring magnitude.
1855	
1856	  Extremeness Aversion adds a stopping rule to Anchoring-and-Adjustment based on perceived
1857	
1858	anchor extremity, hypothesizing adjustment stops when anchors judged “too extreme” (Lewis et al.
1859	
1860	2019). Contrary to this claim, meta-analytic evidence reveals no reliable extremity moderation.
1861	
1862	One limitation is the theory provides little insight into what qualities make an anchor feel more
1863	
1864	extreme other than it’s extremity and the direction. The sense of extremity is a continuum and
1865	
1866	requires explicit prediction about what elements of anchors produce perceived extremity.
1867	
1868	  Noise Theory links representational noise to the plausible-range-mechanism within Anchoring-
1869	
1870	and-Adjustment, offering a formal link between uncertainty and bias (Lee and Morewedge 2022).
1871	
1872	While higher noise, which is operationalized via lower domain knowledge, correlates with larger
1873	
1874	effect sizes in our meta-analysis, the theory treats noise as a static individual trait and does not
1875	
1876	specify how anchor informativeness (e.g., random vs. diagnostic) modulates noise parameters. Joint
1877	
1878	manipulations of knowledge level and anchor type, accompanied by process measures of internal
1879	
1880	variability, are needed to test the theory’s core assumptions.

1882	 5.2.   Guidance for Theory Development
1883	
1884	In the sections that follow, we consider the aforementioned issues with existing theories and outline
1885	
1886	paths forward for testing theory-relevant salience, inference, memory, and depth of processing
1887	
1888	moderators.
1889	
1890	  5.2.1.    Salience. While there has already been sufficient work regarding incidental anchoring
1891	
1892	(Klein et al. 2018), there has been far less attention on temporal delays between the anchor and
1893	
1894	judgment (Mussweiler 2001, Yoon and Fong 2019), optimal exposure time, and types of exposure
1895	
1896	for maximizing anchoring effects. Existing theories differ in their reliance on lower-level versus
1897	
1898	higher-level cognitions. For example, in terms of lower-level cognitions, Numeric Priming and Scale
1899	
1900	Distortion merely require perception of stimuli. On the other hand, Selective Accessibility requires
1901	
1902	higher-level cognitions through explicit hypothesis testing, and Extremeness Aversion involves an
1903	
1904	intermediary judgment of what makes something “extreme.” In principle, different amounts of
1905	
1906	delay manipulate the relative salience of the anchor in decision-makers’ percept. Further, while
1907	
1908	evidence from the meta-analysis suggests that anchoring effects do not appear reliable with inci-
1909	
1910	dental/primed exposure, what is the minimum amount of exposure/salience needed to produce a
1911	
1912	reliable effect?
1913	
1914	  5.2.2.    Inference. How and when people draw inferences across contexts remains a key direc-
1915	
1916	tion for future research. Numerous instructions and manipulations have aimed to separate anchor-
1917	
1918	ing from a conversational inference interpretation (Schwarz 1994, Grice 1975) by signaling, explic-
1919	
1920	itly or implicitly, that the anchor lacks diagnostic information. But, the argument for inference
1921	
1922	making is that decision-makers use inferential cues because more often than not, information is
1923	
1924	presented for a reason (Grice 1975). Several key questions remain: which inferences arise under
1925	
1926	different presentations, how does the similarity between anchor and target shape those inferences,
1927	
1928	and how does similarity modulate bias? For instance, although a tree-height anchor may not affect
1929	
1930	tree-count estimates, it could subtly inform age judgments because of actual or perceived real-
1931	
1932	world correlations, which would be a result that is inconsistent with both the Scale Distortion and
1933	
1934	Selective Accessibility accounts.
1935	                                                 36
1936	   To clarify these processes, we advocate applying the minimalist coherence-gap hypothesis pro-
1937	
1938	posed by McKoon and Ratcliff (1992), which posits that individuals generate only the simplest
1939	
1940	inference needed to make sense of the world. In anchoring, encountering “3,500 miles” in a compar-
1941	
1942	ison question leads to the minimal inference that the number has some relevance to the true value.
1943	
1944	Future studies should systematically vary anchor informativeness (e.g., random vs. market-based),
1945	
1946	dimensional overlap, and framing, while collecting real-time inference data (e.g. think-aloud proto-
1947	
1948	cols or inference-elicitation tasks). Such designs will reveal when anchors become diagnostic cues
1949	
1950	and how those inferences drive anchoring across theoretical perspectives.
1951	
1952	  5.2.3.   Memory. While the meta-analysis suggests total knowledge has a weak negative cor-
1953	
1954	relation with anchoring, there remain numerous theoretically insightful moderators regarding the
1955	
1956	connection between the type of knowledge and anchoring. For example, does it matter whether the
1957	
1958	anchor concerns something that is knowable (e.g., river length) versus something that is unknow-
1959	
1960	able (e.g., final sale price of a house) at the moment of the judgment (i.e., epistemic vs. aleatory
1961	
1962	uncertainty; Tannenbaum et al. 2017)? There may also be key differences between episodic and
1963	
1964	semantic knowledge (Tulving 2002). For example, in the context of Seattle’s highest summer tem-
1965	
1966	perature, the impact of a high anchor may have a stronger impact on someone who has lived
1967	
1968	through a Seattle summer (i.e., episodic) relative to someone with only semantic knowledge of
1969	
1970	Seattle’s weather. These distinctions may also help unpack what anchors are considered extreme,
1971	
1972	which remains relevant for such theories as Extremeness Aversion and Selective Accessibility. More
1973	
1974	broadly, investigating the type of knowledge activated in memory can help refine almost all theories
1975	
1976	of anchoring as most rely on or make predictions about the range of plausible values.
