1979	
1980	flated into subsequent judgments, then in what ways do slower, more deliberative, regulatory
1981	
1982	aspects of cognition (e.g., System 2 processing) play into their use (Evans 2008)? As discussed
1983	
1984	above, existing theories differ in how elaborative their mechanisms are. More thorough testing
1985	
1986	of moderators such as cognitive load and incentives are necessary for understanding what is the

1989	
1990	nisms such moderators as incentives operate (e.g., effort maximization, strategy adoption; Arkes
1991	
1992	1991). For example, investigators might explore a continuum of no, low, moderate, and high load
1993	
1994	rather than just no load versus high load. This type of investigation could, for example, speak
1995

1997

2130	5.3.   Guidance for Practitioners
2131	
2132	We make three recommendations for practitioners who may attempt to use anchors in managerial
2133	
2134	settings. The first direction concerns finding “optimal” values to use in policy and firm settings.
2135	
2136	Currently, there is very little research attempting to quantify the effect so that practitioners can
2137	
2138	select optimal anchors (e.g., how extreme an anchor value should be; Turner and Schley 2016).
2139	
2140	Second, we would also encourage practitioners to explore which features of their particular decision-
2141	
2142	making context make an anchor appear more or less diagnostic. Moderators related to dimension
2143	
2144	and transparent randomness had some of the largest effect sizes in the meta-analysis. Understanding
2145	                                               40
2146	 how these moderators operate and their boundary conditions is necessary for developing effective
2147	
2148	anchor-based interventions for organizations and policy agents. Third, we encourage caution when
2149	
2150	using anchors. While negative effects were rare (7.5% of effect sizes), it would be prudent for
2151	
2152	practitioners to systematically identify under what conditions those negative effects occur.

2154	6.   Conclusion
2155	50 years ago, researchers asked participants about the percentage of African countries in the United
2156	
2157	Nations (Tversky and Kahneman 1974). Since that investigation, there have been thousands of
2158	
2159	investigations across domains, at least seven theories proposed, multiple replications, and likely
2160	
2161	countless classroom demonstrations. What drives anchoring effects is still not solved, but this
2162	
2163	manuscript organizes the theoretical landscape and the empirical distribution of effects to offer
2164	
2165	clarity and direction for future theoretical and applied research.

== 10.2139/ssrn.4605057
<jats:p>One of the most robust phenomena studied across the social behavioral sciences is numeric anchoring, in which a comparison against a presumed-to-be arbitrary number preceding a judgment can influence a myriad of real-world relevant judgments. The authors meta-analyze this expansive literature containing 2,603 total effect sizes (1,283 comparing high anchors against low anchors), finding a large (Hedges' g = 0.824, 95%&nbsp; CI [0.765, 0.883], I^2 = 93.64%) effect with only a small reduction from publication-bias corrections. Evidence suggests reduced (or null) effects associated with incidental anchoring (i.e., numeric priming), anchors from different dimensions or from random numbers, the presence of incentives or debiasing interventions, and&nbsp; knowledge. The authors provide a comprehensive review of both the empirical and theoretical landscape, and offer recommendations for consolidating the literature, improving theory testing, future development of theory and methods related to anchoring, and guidance for managers attempting to use anchoring effects in strategic and policy decisions.</jats:p>

1737	extent of extremity. Consistent with Smith et al. (2013), decision-makers who were more
1738	knowledgeable about the target judgment exhibited smaller anchoring effects. For
1739	information-processing-related moderators, we find that only incentives reliably reduce the
1740	anchoring effect, but acknowledge some systematic reductions for negative-emotion studies
1741	that warrant further investigation. More extensive moderator analyses and publication bias
1742	details can be found in Online Appendix E. Moderator analyses for the other meta-analytic
1743	databases can be found in Online Appendices F-H.
1744	
1745	                                        Meta-Study
1746	
1747	       To supplement our review and synthesis of the anchoring literature, we also
1748	conducted a meta-study (for reviews on meta-studies see Baribault et al., 2018; DeKay,
1749	Rubinchik, Li, & De Boeck, 2022). While meta-analysis is a powerful tool for efficiently
1750	summarizing the literature, 1) it is correlational in nature, 2) it can lack orthogonality and
1751	comparability across effect sizes, and 3) it faces concerns with publication bias.
1752	Meta-studies offer an environment for testing orthogonal moderators, and a pre-registered
1753	meta-study eliminates the concern of publication bias.
1754	
1755	       Anchoring provides a strong opportunity to test moderation of the effect of interest.
1756	Meta-studies begin with a core design around the effect of interest. In this case, our core
1757	design will be the manipulation of high versus low anchors for a set of general knowledge
1758	questions (e.g., Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995). We then manipulate each of these
1759	moderators across this core design. These moderators are embedded as a micro-study
1760	within a singular large orthogonal structure. Moderators are included as within- or
1761	between-participant factors in the meta-study design. The procedure, participants,
1762	   ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                                                 50
1763	
1764	
1765	  experimental design and primary statistical analyses were pre-registered and can be found
1766	  at (AsPredicted #141242) https://aspredicted.org/Y51_336. All meta-study materials,
1767	  data, analyses, as well as additional robustness checks are provided in Online Appendix I
1768	  on the manuscript’s OSF page:
1769	  https://osf.io/9yduf?view_only=2f433256dd404a5ca83d703c1e1b4d99).

1771	  Participants.
1772	
1773	           We recruited 2001 U.S. adults from Prolific in August 2023 in exchange for ($1.60)
1774	  and randomly assigned them to condition (see Method section below for experimental
1775	  design). We excluded 33 responses who failed any one of three pre-registered attention
1776	  checks. The final sample included 1,968 US adults (Mage = 40.71 years, IQR = 20, 825
1777	  female, 1098 male, 37 non-binary/third gender, and 8 preferred not to specify).
1778	
1779	  Procedure.
1780	
1781	           Participants completed eight anchoring questions in a random order (see Table 7).
1782	  In the meta-study, for each of the eight items, participants first saw a numeric anchor, then
1783	  saw an image containing the anchoring item’s text for their numeric estimate. This image
1784	  was intended to reduce the probability that participants searched for the answer online by
1785	  copying and pasting the question text. Then, lastly, participants indicated their subjective
1786	  knowledge from 1 (not at all knowledgeable) to 7 (extremely knowledgeable) on a subsequent
1787	  page.

1807	
1808	       We included as many moderators as possible based on which moderators could
1809	operate independently of each other. Meta-studies are predicated on an assumption that
1810	the effects of any given moderator are independent of other moderators in the study design
1811	(Baribault et al., 2018; DeKay et al., 2022). This assumption limits the potential anchoring
1812	moderators that could be included. We incorporated moderators within- or
1813	between-participant if they were unlikely to violate independence across the other
1814	conditions of the meta-study. For instance, it would be difficult to manipulate anchor
1815	stimulus and directionality orthogonal to whether the anchor is a primed anchor or not.
1816	That is, while some moderators could easily be applied to standard anchoring tasks, it is
1817	not straightforward how to apply these moderators across numeric primes.
1818	
1819	       Within-subjects we manipulated whether anchors were more precise (i.e., had a .00
1820	at the end of the number or not), and anchor extremity (whether the participants saw the
1821	3rd/97th, 15th/85th, or 30th/70th percentiles). That is, across the eight different
1822	anchoring questions, participants could see more or less extreme, high or low, and more or
1823	less precise anchors. We also measured subjective knowledge for each question.
1824	Between-subjects we manipulated the presence of cognitive load (i.e., whether or not a load
1825	task requesting retention of a letter string was present), debiasing instructions (i.e.,
1826	whether or not participants were told at the start of the study and before each judgment to
1827	avoid anchoring), incentives (i.e., whether or not participants learned they could receive a
1828	$0.50 bonus for being within the 10% closest on a randomly-selected judgment), delay (i.e.,
1829	whether or not there was a page break between the numeric anchor and estimate),
1830	directional anchors (i.e., whether the anchor was in a comparative question to which the
1831	participants responded, or stated the target value was greater or less than the anchor), and
1832	diagnosticity in terms of different target stimulus (e.g., asking the anchor in the context of
1833	brownie-baking or chicken-cooking prior to a numeric estimate about brownie-baking). Full
1834	details of the experimental design, including how each moderator was operationalized, can

2051	Discussion
2052	
2053	                      Below we discuss the consistencies and inconsistencies between the meta-study
2054	results and those of the meta-analysis.
2055	
2056	                      Results consistent with the meta-analytic results. Overall, we observed six
2057	consistent findings between the two approaches on delay, different dimensions, directional
2058	anchors, precision, debiasing, and knowledge. We provide this categorization for efficiency
2059	but caution treating the results as definitively consistent or inconsistent. For example,
2060	while delay had a negative coefficient in the meta-analysis and a positive coefficient in the
2061	 ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                         56
2062	
2063	
2064	meta-study, both estimates included zero in their confidence intervals. Further, we
2065	recognize that although the meta-analysis examined knowledge in terms of objective
2066	knowledge differences, the meta-study employed subjective knowledge. Though these two
2067	may diverge (Alba & Hutchinson, 1987; Carlson, Vincent, Hardesty, & Bearden, 2009),
2068	their relationship with the magnitude of anchoring was consistent in this context.
2069	
2070	       Results inconsistent with the meta-analytic results. Overall, we observed
2071	three clearly inconsistent findings between the two approaches (i.e., extremity, incentives,
2072	and cognitive load). Whereas the meta-analysis indicated little moderation by extremity,
2073	results of the meta-study indicated a large increase in the anchoring effect when the anchors
2074	were more extreme. One important consideration is that the coding of extremity in the
2075	meta-analysis was based on the authors’ explicit or implicit characterization of extremity.
2076	Most studies in our meta-analysis had no explicitly-declared calibration pretest to evaluate
2077	the extent of an anchor’s extremity for their sample population. Further, even within the
2078	meta-study, our characterization of the 3rd and 97th percentiles might not reflect the same
2079	magnitude of extremity as those used in the studies within the meta-analysis. Next, unlike
2080	the meta-analysis, in the meta-study we did not observe incentives attenuate the anchoring
2081	effect. It is possible that the presence of incentives gave no new strategies for addressing
2082	anchoring but instead only increased motivation (see Arkes, 1991). Finally, cognitive load
2083	may have increased effect sizes in the meta-study but not the meta-analysis because of
2084	mono-operation bias (Shadish, Cook, & Campbell, 2002) whereby our particular
2085	operationalization of cognitive load might increase anchoring effects, but this may not be
2086	the case for the myriad of different types of cognitive-load manipulations present across the
2087	anchoring literature that were all coalesced under our cognitive-load variable.
2088	
2089	       Overall, the meta-study provided some results that support the meta-analytic
2090	findings and other results that appeared inconsistent, which might reflect two possibilities.
2091	The first possibility is that the meta-study was not representative of the studies in the
2092	literature. For instance, we used a memory-load task to induce cognitive load, whereas
2093	 ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                         57
2094	
2095	
2096	some studies in the literature used time pressure (e.g., Simonson & Drolet, 2004). In this
2097	way, the meta-study may also suffer from a mono-operation bias in which it only adopts
2098	one manifestation of a given manipulation, and thus its conclusions may be limited to the
2099	approaches we adopted (Shadish et al., 2002). Another dimension of representativeness
2100	could be that the online participants in the meta-study were substantially different than
2101	those across the literature, which included a mixture of field, laboratory, and online
2102	participants. In the Online Appendix E we report coefficients for the exploratory
2103	moderators from the meta-analysis and do see significant moderation as a function of
2104	whether the study was run with an online panel or in-person participants.
2105	
2106	       The second explanation for the inconsistencies could be a combination of publication
2107	bias along with other non-reporting biases relevant to the meta-analytic database. That is,
2108	incomplete reporting of nonsignificant moderation in published studies (i.e., collapsing over
2109	levels of a moderator when reporting results), suppression of failed replications, or other
2110	findings that contradict existing theories could all lead to an artificial inflation or deflation
2111	of effect size differences (Coburn & Vevea, 2015; Vevea, Coburn, & Sutton, 2019). The
2112	advantage of meta-studies is that they give every moderator equivalent opportunity under
2113	the assumption of equivalent operationalization of the manipulations. This means that
2114	results cannot be due to publication incentives or outcome/moderator reporting bias.
2115	
2116	                                     General Discussion
2117	
2118	       How do people make numeric estimates? Whether wondering how much to bid in an
2119	eBay auction, contemplating how many people will support a policy, or assessing how long
2120	the commute to work will take, these estimates have important implications for numerous
2121	decisions. The anchoring literature offers one answer: people use recently-encountered
2122	numeric stimuli as an input to these judgments. Despite the generality of this literature,
2123	there remain numerous unanswered questions.
2124	
2125	       We caution that while our meta-analysis and meta-study are the most
2126	comprehensive exploration of moderators of the anchoring effect to date, the results are by
2127	 ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                               58
2128	
2129	
2130	no means definitive. Anchoring is an extremely broad research area, both conceptually and
2131	substantively. Given the breadth of the anchoring literature, it is necessary to be cautious
2132	about assumptions of generality from studies that involve only a particular anchoring
2133	stimulus and a particular operation of a moderator. As such, we encourage researchers and
2134	practitioners to use the current manuscript as starting-point for future lines of anchoring
2135	research rather than as the catalog of the “average effect size” for each moderator.
2136	
2137	What is an Anchoring Effect?
2138	
2139	       While the anchoring effect is an exceptionally large literature that spans the
2140	behavioral, and related, sciences, its theoretical space is quite fragmented. After 50 years of
2141	research on this phenomenon, there is no one theory that provides a parsimonious
2142	explanation of all of the latent drivers that produce this seminal effect – and there may not
2143	need be one (see below). We suggest that the features of this literature that have facilitated
2144	its proliferation are also what has prevented it from reaching theoretical clarity in terms of

moderators in this section can be thought to influence the amount and type of information
retrieved from memory when making judgments in the presence of anchors.

       Anchor Extremity. Anchor extremity implies that, for a given level of
anchor-relevant knowledge, anchor values further from the median belief will, on average,
be perceived to be more extreme. For example, an anchor about the Chicago Bears scoring
greater than or less than 85 points during the entire 2007 regular football season might
seem reasonable to a non-football fan but might feel extremely low to an avid football fan
 ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                      18


with more judgment-relevant exemplars in memory (Smith, Windschitl, & Bruchmann,
2013). We categorize this under memory because the perception of extremity is derived by
the decision-maker evaluating the anchor against values in their memory. If the anchor
value is outside a plausible range (i.e., perceived to be too extreme), then it may be
discounted for failing to match existing memory representations (Quattrone et al., 1984;
Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell, & Jarvis, 2001). Extant theories mostly have predictions
for this moderator. Anchoring-and-adjustment argues that more extreme anchors may
increase anchoring as long as the anchors are within the decision-maker’s range of plausible
values. Once anchors are outside that range, people will adjust estimates back into the
range (Quattrone et al., 1984). The Attitudinal Perspective, by contrast, suggests extreme
anchors will be discounted and will produce weaker effects, yielding an inverse-U shape by
which anchoring is less effective when the low and high anchors are extreme relative to not
(Wegener et al., 2001). Extremeness Aversion contends people will cease adjustment when
they feel they have moved too far, which leads to larger effect sizes as anchor extremity
increases. Finally, according to he Noise Theory, higher magnitudes, which may be
achieved at more extreme values, should widen the range of plausible values and thus
increase anchoring.




       Knowledge. Experts may have their own heuristics, schema, and background
information (Alba & Hutchinson, 1987; Payne, Bettman, & Johnson, 1993), which may
inform either the use of the correct answer (Wilson et al., 1996, Numeric Priming) or what
values are considered within the range of possible values (Anchoring-and-Adjustment and
Selective Accessibility Mussweiler & Strack, 2000a; Quattrone et al., 1984). Even if they do
not know the exact answer, experts (relative to non-experts) might have a tighter (i.e., less
noisy) distribution of plausible values (C.-Y. Lee & Morewedge, 2022, Noise Theory) or
might use irrelevant anchor information less because they have a sufficient amount of
information already to make the judgment (Smith et al., 2013; Turner & Schley, 2016).

content.content:
ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                        2


                                         Abstract

One of the most robust phenomena studied across the social behavioral sciences is numeric
anchoring, in which a comparison against a presumed-to-be arbitrary number preceding a
judgment can influence a myriad of real-world relevant judgments. The authors
meta-analyze this expansive literature containing 2,603 total effect sizes (1,283 comparing
high anchors against low anchors), finding a large (d = 0.824, 95% CI [0.765, 0.883],
I 2 = 93.64%) effect with only a small reduction from publication-bias corrections. Evidence
suggests reduced (or null) effects associated with incidental anchoring (i.e., numeric
priming), anchors from different dimensions or from random numbers, the presence of
incentives or debiasing interventions, and knowledge. The authors supplement the
meta-analysis with a pre-registered meta-study (N = 1,968) comparing high against low
anchors and find similar moderation by anchors from different dimensions, extremity,
cognitive load, knowledge, and debiasing but not presence of incentives. The authors
provide a comprehensive review of both the empirical and theoretical landscape, and offer
recommendations for consolidating the literature, improving theory testing, future
development of theory and methods related to anchoring, and guidance for managers
attempting to use anchoring effects in strategic and policy decisions.
meta-analysis, we did not have enough precision in the literature to tease apart the exact
roles of the anchor stimulus/dimension, but encourage further exploration. In particular,
how similar/different (Evers, Imas, & Kang, 2022) does the anchor need to be to generate
an inference that it is a diagnostic cue for the judgment?

       These inferences also likely differ between the reviewed anchoring paradigms. For
paradigm one, there are likely not a wide array of inferences because the paradigm is
controlled and simplistic. Thus, for paradigm one, we encourage researchers to explore how
the inference affects beliefs both about the central tendency of the anchor and the
distribution of possible true values (Turner & Schley, 2016). This is relevant to a range of
anchoring theories. For example, according to the Attitudinal Perspective (Wegener et al.,
2010), anchoring occurring via central route processing should influence the strength of
 ANCHORING META-ANALYSIS AND META-STUDY                                                          64


that belief which should present itself as having a tighter distribution of potential values.
This range of potential values is also relevant to Anchoring-and-Adjustment (Quattrone et
al., 1984), Extremeness Aversion (Lewis et al., 2019), and Noise Theory (C.-Y. Lee &
Morewedge, 2022). It is also possible to explore the variance of beliefs not only within a
focal judgment, but across an entire domain. For example, how does an anchor about the
weight of a giraffe influence beliefs about the weights of other animals (i.e., Scale Distortion
management, economics, and marketing), the results on boundary conditions in this
manuscript suggest three recommendations for practitioners who may attempt to use
anchors in managerial settings. The first direction concerns finding “optimal” values to use
in policy and firm settings (Goswami & Urminsky, 2016). That is, despite the prevalence of
anchoring, there is very little research attempting to quantify the effect so that
practitioners can select optimal anchors (Turner & Schley, 2016). This question of optimal
anchor values relates to anchor extremity: at what threshold do anchors no longer lead to
assimilation? In the meta-analysis we found no consistent moderation of extremity but
found an increase with more extreme anchors in the meta-study. To understand the role of
extremity a more effective study design requires assessing anchor values at each level of a
baseline distribution – rather than at just the 3rd/97th, 15th/85th, and 30th/70th
percentiles. This would offer a fuller picture by mapping the extremity continuum and
identifying optimal anchor values.

Title:           Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in item-based anchoring
Pages:           18

13	Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in
14	item-based anchoring
15	David J. Young a,b, Maarten Speekenbrink b, M. Irmak Buyukyildirim b,
16	Angus C.H. Chung b, Monty Gwynne b, Fredrika Hillström b, Bryan K.H. Hui b ,
17	Eunice Shing b, Adam J.L. Harris b,*
18	a
19	    Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom
20	b
21	    Department of Experimental Psychology, University College London, United Kingdom
22

26	A R T I C L E I N F O                                     A B S T R A C T
27	
28	Keywords:                                                 Anchoring is a prominent judgment bias which causes people’s estimates of uncertain quantities
29	Anchoring                                                 to assimilate towards recently encountered values. Here, we ask whether items can cause
30	Judgment                                                  anchoring – will the question “Does a handheld flashlight torch cost more or less than a laptop?”
31	Bias
32	                                                          induce anchoring in the same way as “Does a handheld flashlight torch cost more or less than
33	Item-based anchoring
34	Anchoring-by-items
35	                                                          £500”? We present evidence from ten studies suggesting that it can, and that perceptions of the
36	Selective accessibility                                   value of the anchor item (e.g., the laptop) are also anchored. In other words, estimates for both
37	                                                          items being compared assimilate towards each other. We also find that low value items are
38	                                                          anchored more strongly than high value items. Overall, there is evidence for a small anchoring-
39	                                                          by-items effect (Hedge’s g = 0.25), which we suggest previous studies may have been under­
40	                                                          powered to detect. Among existing theories of anchoring, Selective Accessibility would appear to
41	                                                          provide the best account of the data.
42	
43	
44	
45	
46	1. Introduction
47	
48	    How much would you pay for a torch? The answer to this question depends on a variety of factors: What sort of torch? How much do
49	you want a torch? How much money do you have? Research in Judgment and Decision Making has shown that the amount you are
50	willing to pay is likely to also depend upon a variety of contextual features. One of these contextual effects has been termed Anchoring.
51	Research on the Anchoring effect informs us that a shop assistant asking whether you thought the torch was worth more or less than
52	£300 is likely to be able to eventually sell the torch for a higher price than if they first asked if you thought the same torch was worth
53	more or less than £10. People’s estimates of uncertain quantities (the value of this torch) reliably assimilate towards previously
54	considered values, which have come to be called ‘anchors’ (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). But what if the shop assistant had asked you
55	if you thought the torch was worth more or less than a laptop computer, or a small pack of batteries? Would this have a similar in­
56	fluence on your perception of the torch’s value? The current paper tests for such ‘item-based anchoring’ effects.
57	    Anchoring is a prominent judgment phenomenon (for a review see Bahník et al., 2022; for meta-analyses see Röseler & Schütz,
58	2022; Schley & Weingarten, 2025). In typical demonstrations, people answer a comparative estimation question which asks them to
59	compare the value of an uncertain target item against a specified anchor; they then answer an absolute estimation question which
60	
61	
62	
63	    * Corresponding author.
64	      E-mail address: [email redacted] (A.J.L. Harris).
65	
66	https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796
67	Received 19 November 2024; Received in revised form 9 March 2026; Accepted 9 March 2026
68	Available online 21 March 2026
69	0010-0285/© 2026 The Author(s).          Published by Elsevier Inc.     This is an open access article under the CC BY license
70	(http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
71	 D.J. Young et al.                                                                                        Cognitive Psychology 164 (2026) 101796
72	
73	
74	requires them to estimate the value of the target item, with the common result being that this estimate is biased towards the anchor.
75	Strack and Mussweiler (1997), for example, asked people to estimate Gandhi’s age upon his death after first asking them to judge
76	whether it was higher or lower than either 140, or 9. After being given the high anchor of 140, people’s average estimate was 67, but
77	with the low anchor of 9, the average estimate was significantly lower, at 50. The anchoring effect has been shown to influence
78	numerous important judgments, such as criminal sentencing (e.g., Bystranowski et al., 2021; Englich, 2006; Englich et al., 2006),
79	awarding compensation (Robbennolt & Studebaker, 1999), financial negotiations (e.g., Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001), price judg­
80	ments (e.g., Jung, Perfecto, & Nelson, 2016), economic forecasting (e.g., Campbell & Sharpe, 2009), and credit card payments (e.g.,
81	Navarro-Martinez et al., 2011; Stewart, 2009). There is no doubt that anchoring is a robust phenomenon – in a large meta-analysis,
82	Schley and Weingarten (2025) found an average effect size for the difference in estimates obtained following high vs low anchors of
83	Cohen’s d = 0.876, and anchoring effects proved consistently replicable in a Many Labs replication project (Klein et al., 2014). Despite
84	discussion of potential adaptive (Harvey, 2011) or resource-rational (Lieder et al., 2018a, 2018b) accounts of anchoring, it is typically
85	considered to be a judgment bias, particularly as anchoring can occur even when participants know the anchors were generated
86	randomly, and therefore have not been encountered as realistic proposals for the target value (for examples see e.g., Englich et al.,
87	2006; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
88	    Prototypical anchoring studies (such as those cited above) refer to the assimilation of a numeric judgment to a numeric anchor,
89	which participants are required to consider in relation to the target judgment (“Was Gandhi older or younger than 9 years old when he
90	died?”). Researchers have also, however, deviated from this classic paradigm. Wilson et al. (1996), for example, introduced ‘basic
91	anchoring’, whereby a numeric anchor was provided in an unrelated task, without reference to the target judgment. Oppenheimer
92	et al. (2008) extended the conceptual distance of the anchor from the target, and found that participants’ judgments of the length of the
93	Mississippi River and Honolulu’s average July temperature were influenced by the drawing of a long or short line (higher judgments
94	following a long line than a short line). Instead of testing the effect of a numeric anchor on numeric judgments of a target stimulus,
95	Frederick and Mochon (2012, Studies 1 & 2A) required participants to select a stimulus to match a particular numeric value (e.g., an
96	animal that weighs 1,000 lbs).
97	    Our present studies are faithful to the tradition that the target judgment is first compared with an anchor, but our anchor is an item,
98	rather than a number. These studies follow Mochon and Frederick (2013, see also, Bahník et al., 2019; Chapman & Johnson, 1994) who
99	asked participants questions like “Does a camera cost more or less than a pack of AA batteries” and “Does a camera cost more or less
100	than a washing machine?” and did not observe significant anchoring effects. This demonstrable variety in paradigms introduced to test
101	‘anchoring’ effects raises the question: ‘what are the defining characteristics of an anchoring effect?’
102	    As is apparent from the examples above, and the variety of extant theories of anchoring, the term ‘anchoring’ might be considered a
103	category comprising multiple distinct effects (see also Bahník et al., 2022; Frederick & Mochon, 2012; Kahneman, 2011; Schley &
104	Weingarten, 2025; Simmons et al., 2010). The one feature that is common to all the studies cited in the previous paragraphs is
105	assimilation. We then contend that the question of whether an assimilation effect should be termed anchoring or not should be
106	influenced by the utility of that categorisation for either theoretical or applied purposes. Indeed, we surmise that the ubiquitous use of
107	the term ‘anchoring’ to categorise a variety of potentially disparate effects in the literature likely reflects a useful applied purpose:
108	describing the phenomenon to individuals outside of academia and highlighting the relevance of assimilation effects in areas such as
109	retail. In the present paper, we follow Mochon and Frederick (2013) in including the specific item-based effects we test here within the
110	category of ‘anchoring effects’. While it is certainly debatable whether item-based anchoring should really be considered a type of
111	anchoring, our decision to do so stems from three considerations: firstly, by following the example of previous studies that have studied
112	item-based anchoring in referring to it as a kind of anchoring, we avoid bringing confusion into the literature by having papers which
113	study the same phenomenon using different names; secondly, our studies closely follow traditional numerical anchoring designs, but
114	simply use items instead of numbers as anchors; finally, we agree with Mochon and Frederick (2013) that anchoring-by-items is a
115	natural prediction of one of the most prominent theories of prototypical anchoring effects, Selective Accessibility (Strack & Muss­
116	weiler, 1997). Mochon and Frederick’s (2013) failure to observe evidence for item-based anchoring was one empirical result sup­
117	porting their advancement of the Scale Distortion Theory (Frederick & Mochon, 2012).
118	
119	
120	1.1. Selective accessibility and item-based anchoring
121	
122	   Selective Accessibility (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999, 2000a, 2000b, 2001; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; see also Chapman & Johnson,
123	1994, 1999) proposes that when people are faced with the initial comparative judgment question in an anchoring experiment (e.g.,
124	“Does a camera cost more or less than $900?”), they employ a positive test strategy (Klayman & Ha, 1987) and seek to retrieve in­
125	formation about the stimulus which is consistent with the anchor (the camera having a value of $900). This question therefore prompts
126	participants to retrieve information about high specification cameras (e.g., SLRs). When participants are then asked how much cameras
127	actually cost, the previously-retrieved information is primed, and is therefore selectively more accessible than other information about
128	the stimulus when the participant makes this judgment. Consequently, participants think about more expensive cameras and therefore
129	provide a price estimate that is higher than in the absence of the comparative question. Were people given a low anchor of $6 to begin
130	with, they would retrieve examples of, for example, cheap disposable cameras when answering the comparative question, with
131	
132	
133	
134	
135	                                                                    2
136	 D.J. Young et al.                                                                                         Cognitive Psychology 164 (2026) 101796
137	
138	
139	absolute price estimates therefore lower. According to the Selective Accessibility account then, the initial comparative question dis­
140	torts people’s perception of the target stimulus. There seems no reason why this wouldn’t also occur with item-anchors. If people are
141	asked “Does a camera cost more or less than a washing machine?”, their search for hypothesis-consistent information should still
142	prompt them to retrieve examples of cameras which are quite expensive. But if asked “Does a camera cost more or less than a pack of
143	AA batteries”, this should prompt retrieval of much cheaper cameras, thus producing an anchoring effect.
144	    To date, however, no study has reported significant anchoring-by-items effects, with three null results reported (Bahník et al., 2019;
145	Chapman & Johnson, 1994 [Experiment 2]; Mochon & Frederick, 2013 [Experiment 1]). As we explain below, however, we believe a
146	closer inspection of the relationship between anchoring-by-items and the Selective Accessibility theory still means it is an open
147	question whether anchoring-by-items occurs. We believe that it is important to thoroughly test this phenomenon for two reasons.
148	Firstly, as previously mentioned, we agree with Mochon and Frederick (2013) that anchoring-by-items would appear to be a natural
149	prediction of Selective Accessibility. Given some failures to replicate process evidence for Selective Accessibility (Harris et al., 2019),
150	ascertaining the existence or otherwise of anchoring-by-items is informative for the status of the theory. Secondly, our investigation
151	sheds light on the scope and boundary conditions of (the category of) anchoring effects.
152	    Although none of the previously conducted studies have observed significant anchoring-by-items effects, all three returned results
153	numerically consistent with an effect, meaning it is possible they each failed to detect a real, but small, effect (although their designs
154	are too different to permit a meta-analysis). Anchoring-by-item effect sizes might be predicted to be smaller than numeric anchoring
155	effect sizes for two reasons. Firstly, items have less-specific values than numeric values. A positive test strategy will therefore not have
156	to recruit such extreme information as if the anchor is a number representing the mean value of the item (on the influence of anchor
157	variability on anchoring effects, see Turner & Schley, 2016, and especially their Fig. 1). Secondly (and relatedly), on a Selective
158	Accessibility account, the assumption is that information is first recruited that a camera costs the same as the anchor. Where the anchor
159	is $900, such a positive test strategy entails consideration of expensive cameras. Where the anchor is a washing machine, however, the
160	positive test strategy might result in consideration of expensive cameras, or cheap washing machines, or both. In either of the latter two
161	cases, one would predict a smaller anchoring effect on estimates of the camera’s price.
162	    Harris and Speekenbrink (2016) proposed the latter bidirectional property of anchoring-by-items as a potential explanation for why
163	Mochon and Frederick (2013) did not observe an anchoring-by-item effect. Harris and Speekenbrink argued that a test of anchoring-
164	by-items required testing for anchoring both on the target (camera) and anchor (washing machine) items, as it could be the case that
165	estimates of only one of these items is biased by the comparison. The smaller predicted effect also implies that more participants will be
166	required for item-based anchor studies than numeric anchoring studies.
167	    When highlighting the requirement to investigate anchoring-by-items by testing absolute estimates of both the target and the
168	anchor, Harris and Speekenbrink (2016) did not see this ‘Position’ factor (target vs. anchor) as the key moderator of the effect. Rather,
169	they proposed that the more variable stimulus would be anchored more. This follows Turner and Schley’s (2016) Anchor Integration
170	Model, which argues that information about the value distributions of the target stimulus and the anchor are integrated in a Bayesian
171	fashion by using inverse-variance weighting to produce a ‘posterior’ distribution from which estimates of the target’s absolute value
172	are drawn; consequently, this posterior distribution lies closer to the less-variable original distribution.
173	    Let us clarify what we mean by variability in the present context. Our assumption is that, for any given target judgment (e.g., the
174	cost of a camera), participants can draw upon information from memory to inform their judgment, but this information can usually
175	support a range of possible different values. Within that range, the available information makes certain values appear more plausible
176	than others. This can be modelled as each participant possessing a probability distribution across different possible values, with higher
177	probability assigned to more plausible values. There is therefore variability in the range of possible values that a single participant
178	might consider the item to have – and it is this ‘within-person’ variability which is of critical relevance.
179	    The variability in a probability distribution of possible values may derive from variation in the stimulus’ exemplars – for any given
180	stimulus, there may be different examples of it, which have different corresponding values (e.g., the stimulus ‘camera’ is consistent
181	with high-end wildlife photography SLR cameras, as well as cheap disposable cameras). Alternatively, variability can derive from
182	variation in a stimulus’ features – for a given example of an item, we may be able to construe of it in different ways by focusing more or
183	less on features which imply it has a high or low value (e.g., a camera is simultaneously a high-tech piece of equipment [expensive
184	feature] and a common consumer item that many people are able to afford [cheaper]). We also note that a lack of information
185	(epistemic uncertainty), either in terms of not possessing knowledge of relevant exemplars and features, or not knowing how relevant
186	exemplars and features translate onto the judgment scale, can also lead to more variable value distributions. Without specific infor­
187	mation accessible to make judgments, people may fall back on higher-order information (e.g., category information about the general
188	prices of consumer technology, see also Mussweiler & Strack, 2000a, 2000b), permitting a wider range of possible values. In the
189	present context, we do not anticipate that the source of the variability is of critical importance. Rather, we hold that the relevant
190	consideration is whether there is variability in the possible range of values that the participant might estimate the target stimulus to
191	possess. There is prior empirical evidence from the numeric anchoring literature to support our supposition about the influence of an
192	item’s uncertainty on how much it is anchored. Turner and Schley (2016, Experiment 2), for example, find that when participants
193	estimate the value of the target item before and after comparing it to an anchor value, those who report lower confidence in their initial
194	estimate, and therefore have more uncertainty about its value, show stronger anchoring effects.
195	
196	
197

203	   In this article, we present 10 studies which test for item-based anchoring effects. We test two primary hypotheses which reflect,
204	respectively, Harris and Speekenbrink (2016)’s speculations that: (a) both items compared in the comparative question can be
205	anchored; and (b) the amount an item is anchored is in direct proportion to its perceived variability:
206	   H1. Items can cause anchoring effects (on either the anchor or the target).
207	   H2. Anchoring effects (on either the anchor or the target) will be greater, the more variable individuals’ estimates are.
208	
209	2. Method
210	
211	    Designs, analysis plans, and hypotheses were pre-registered for all studies, apart from 5 and 6, though we deviated from these plans
212	at some points. The wording of the pre-registered hypotheses differed slightly in some of the original documents, but for ease of
213	presentation, we test the same hypotheses for all studies. We note that all pre-registered studies included versions of H1, and Studies
214	1–4 included hypotheses intended to represent H2.1 Studies 9–10 were not designed to test H2. All of our pre-registrations, data, and
215	scripts can be found via the OSF (https://osf.io/2a9nz/?view_only=521149d6c0fe40d1ac331073dd36bf43).2
216	    A meta-analysis was not the original plan for our investigation. After Study 1 returned strong evidence of an anchoring-by-items
217	effect, our next studies were designed to test moderators of the anchoring-by-items effect. Some of these subsequent studies did
218	not, however, replicate the effect. We therefore redirected our efforts towards testing the robustness of the effect by collecting more
219	data and conducting a meta-analysis. In the main text, we therefore gloss over some differences between the studies for the sake of
220	focusing on the evidence for the overall anchoring-by-items effect. These differences are, however, highlighted in footnotes and further
221	explored in the Supplementary Materials.
222	    Eight of our 10 studies employed the same novel design, therefore we begin this section with an explanation of this design before
223	explaining how Studies 9 and 10 differ. We then give information about our participants and procedure.
224

226	2.1. Design
227	
228	2.1.1. Independent variables
229	
230	2.1.1.1. Studies 1–8. Studies 1–8 employed a novel experimental design, which we term the “High-Low” design. Participants
231	compared the value of a High-Value stimulus to a Low-Value stimulus (classified based on baseline estimates), before being asked to
232	estimate the absolute value of one of those stimuli (the ‘critical stimulus’). Fig. 1 shows how the design differs to the “classic” design of
233	numerical anchoring studies and illustrates predicted anchoring-by-items effects. Like typical anchoring studies, each trial consists of
234	two questions, a comparative estimation question (“CQ”), followed by an absolute estimation question (“AQ”). Whereas in classic
235	anchoring studies the comparative question would ask participants whether the value of some property of a stimulus is greater or lower
236	than a particular value on a given scale (e.g. “Is the average annual temperature in Norway greater or lower than 28◦ C?”), our
237	comparative questions ask participants to compare the value of two items (“Is the average annual temperature in Norway greater or
238	lower than the average annual temperature in Jamaica?”). The absolute estimation question that follows then asks the participant to
239	estimate the value of one of the items − the ‘Critical Item’.
240	    Our Position variable represents the order in which the items are mentioned in the question. The first item occupies the ‘Target’
241	position, and the second item occupies the ‘Anchor’ position, mirroring the standard presentation of anchors and targets in numeric
242	anchoring studies.
243	    When items are used as anchors, the comparison question could ask about either of the two items – it could be “What is the average
244	annual temperature in Norway?” or “What is the average annual temperature in Jamaica?”. We give participants multiple trials so that
245	we can counterbalance the Position (Target vs Anchor) and Value (High vs Low) of the Critical Item. Our assumption is that the act of
246	comparison will force estimates of the Critical Item to assimilate towards the value of the Non-Critical Item (as in Fig. 1 Panel B). If the
247	Critical Item is Low-Value, the Non-Critical Item will be High-Value, and so estimates of Low-Value items should be drawn upwards;
248	conversely, if the Critical Item is High-Value, the Non-Critical Item must be Low-Value, and so estimates of High-Value items should be
249	pulled downwards. Our expectation is that this will occur irrespective of the Position of the Critical Item, as stated in H1.

312	2.1.2. Randomization
313	   In Studies 1–6, 9 and 10, we used a Latin square to partially randomize the allocation of stimuli across trials and conditions (see
314	Supplementary Material 6 for details). In Studies 7 and 8, the study was programmed such that stimuli were allocated randomly for
315	each trial (without replacement) from the pool of possible stimuli (4 High-Value and 4 Low-Value).

317	2.1.3. Variability
318	    H2 states that “anchoring effects will be larger the more variable individuals’ estimates are” (this was not pre-registered to be tested
319	in Studies 9 and 10). Pilot testing for Study 1 revealed that orthogonally manipulating Value and Variability, as we had originally
320	intended, was going to be extremely challenging (potentially impossible with non-artificial stimuli). In our Pilot testing, Value and
321	Variability were almost perfectly correlated. 18 people provided ‘best guess’, minimum, and maximum estimates of the price of 41
322	consumer products. The correlation between mean ‘best guesses’ and the median difference between maximum and minimum esti­
323	mates was r(39) = 0.94, p < 0.001. This relationship is consistent with Weber’s law and the principle of scalar variability (e.g., Dehaene
324	& Marques, 2002; Lambert, 1978; see also Lee & Morewedge, 2022).
325	    In our studies, therefore, we considered Value a proxy for Variability. In individual studies, this directly confounds effects of
326	Variability with potential direct effects of Value. In order to address this confound, across studies we used different stimulus domains,
327	with opposing relationships between Value and Variability. Specifically, Studies 1, 2, 6, and 7 used the prices of products as stimuli
328	(where Value and Variability are positively correlated), whereas Studies 3, 5, and 8 use the temperatures of countries, and Study 4 used
329	probability judgments. For temperatures, there is a negative relationship between Value and Variability, since the temperatures of hot
330	(High-Value) countries are less variable because they tend to be nearer the Equator and therefore less seasonal, leading to less tem­
331	perature variation throughout the year than colder countries. Indeed, for the countries featured in these studies there is a negative
332	correlation between their average annual temperature and the range of their monthly mean temperatures, r(12) = − 0.73, p = 0.003,
333	according to an analysis we conducted of World Bank data from 1991 to 2020 (World Bank, n.d.) – see Supplementary Materials 2 for
334	details.
335	    The Probability domain (where participants estimated the probability that people from different countries would possess particular

356	participants, who made absolute judgments in the absence of any anchors (see Fig. 3). For our main analysis, we began by finding the
357	Percentile Rank (“Rank”) of each estimate within the distribution of calibration estimates for the same stimulus (following Jacowitz &

360	experimental estimate, F is the frequency of estimates equal to the experimental estimate, and n is the number of estimates (all these
361	quantities include the experimental estimate itself). Experimental estimates equal to the calibration median generally score 50, though
362	the exact score also depends on the number of ties. Anchoring predicts that Ranks should be higher for Low-Value critical stimuli
363	(which are predicted to be anchored upwards by comparison with High-Value stimuli) than High-Value critical stimuli (which are
364	predicted to be anchored downwards by comparison with Low-Value stimuli).

379	2.2. Stimuli
380	
381	   The stimuli used in each study are shown in Tables 1 and 2, along with summary information of calibration estimates. In Studies
382	1–8, the median estimates of all High-Value stimuli were above the 85th percentile of estimates for every Low-Value stimulus.
383	Similarly, the median estimate of every Low-Value stimulus was below the 15th percentile of estimates for every High-Value stimulus.
384	The above represents our adaptation of Jacowitz and Kahneman’s (1994) criterion that high anchors should have values above the
385	85th percentile of the target stimulus’ distribution of value estimates, and low anchors below the 15th percentile. For Study 10, the
386	anchors were always below the 15th percentile of the critical stimuli or above the 85th percentile, but this was slightly violated in some
387	pairings for Study 9.

395	Material 3). Our calibration studies were completed by 957 participants in total, but four were excluded – one from Study 7, for
396	participating twice, and three from Study 10 for providing a year of birth which did not match their stated age, leaving total N = 953
397	(see Table 3 for demographic details). Participants were drawn from the same population as for the main studies. Specifically, the
398	Study 1 calibration data were collected through in-person surveys on University College London campus, while for all other studies it

400	    For Studies 1–4 and 9, calibration data were collected prior to each main study. This was so that we could confirm whether the
401	chosen stimuli satisfied our requirements (see Stimuli section above). We subsequently realized the potential for a confounding in­
402	fluence of this temporal delay. The potential for such a confound was increased where calibration data were (for some studies)
403	collected either side of the university Christmas break. Not only might calibration estimates of temperatures be affected by current
404	weather conditions, but estimates of prices might be affected by the recency, versus imminence, of the largest consumer event of the
405	year. Studies 5–8 addressed this potential confound, by obtaining calibration estimates concurrently with the experimental estimates;
406	participants were randomly assigned to either provide calibration or experimental estimates.

508	
509	   After choosing to participate, participants read the task instructions and provided informed consent. Participants then completed

512	– 100 (“definitely WILL happen”) scale (see Supplementary Material 3 for exact question wordings, and our OSF project for the surveys
513	themselves). After their trials, participants provided demographic data and were debriefed.

519	design. We then conducted a number of exploratory analyses to determine aggregate effects and explore robustness. We summarise the
520	evidence for each hypothesis in turn.

3.1. Hypothesis 1

3.1.1. Value × Position ANOVAs
   In all but one study (Study 9), a numerical trend consistent with an anchoring effect was observed – the Low-Value stimuli’s es­
timates had higher ranks than the High-Value stimuli’s estimates. This trend was significant in five studies, with effects ranging from
Cohen’s f = 0.19 (small) to 0.89 (very large). The reverse trend observed in Study 9 was not significant. Table 4 shows the mean Ranks

                                                                                                                     10
 D.J. Young et al.                                                                                              Cognitive Psychology 164 (2026) 101796




Fig. 4. The distributions of ranks for high and low value items, across studies 1–10, with means and 95% CIs shown by the points at the bottom.




by Value, and the main effect statistics for each individual study.

3.1.2. Exploratory analyses
    To determine whether the studies provide evidence for an overall anchoring-by-items effect, we aggregated the data from all ten
studies into one dataset. Low-Value stimuli had higher Ranks (M = 55.81, SD = 28.05; one-sample t-test [H0: μ = 50]: t[2286] = 9.912,
p < 0.001, d = 0.21 [0.17, 0.25]) than High-Value stimuli (M = 48.79, SD = 28.79; one-sample t-test [H0: μ = 50]: t[2286] = 2.010, p =
0.045, d = 0.042 [0.001, 0.083]) – see Fig. 4. To test whether this was a reliable difference, we calculated each person’s mean Rank for
High- and Low-Value items, collapsing across Position,5 then compared them using a paired-samples t-test, finding a small but sig­
nificant effect, t(1352) = 7.31, p < 0.001, d = 0.20 [0.14, 0.25].6 Given the heterogeneity in designs across studies, this is the clearest
way to test the overall effect.
    We then performed a meta-analysis of the effect size across all 10 studies. We again found the average Rank of each person’s es­
timates for High-Value items, and their average Rank for estimates of Low-Value items, collapsing across Position. We then calculated
the paired-samples Hedge’s g and standard error of the difference between the two for each study. The patterns of significance matched
those in the ANOVAs above, with the exception of Study 4, which became non-significant (see Fig. 5). Using a random-effects model
and the Hartung-Knapp method to account for between-study variance in effect sizes (see Jackson et al., 2017), we obtained a meta-
analytic Hedge’s g of 0.25 [0.05, 0.45]7 – see Fig. 3.

3.1.3. Robustness checks
   We test whether the anchoring effect is present in several notable subsets of our studies, using the t-test approach described above.

 6
    As a non-parametric alternative, we also ran a Wilcoxon signed rank test, which also found a significant result W=554877, p<.001. Comparing
whether the mean rank for Low- and High-Value stimuli was significantly different from 50 using one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, both were:
Low-Value W = 1610771, p < 0.001, High-Value W = 1364224, p = 0.046.
  7
    We used the R (R Core Team, 2022) package {meta} (Balduzzi et al., 2019), specifically the functions metagen() and forest(). We used restricted
maximum likelihood to estimate between-study variance. Without the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, we find the same result with a narrower con­
fidence interval, g = 0.25 [0.09, 0.42].

Namely, for each participant, we calculate the mean Ranks of their estimates for High-Value and, separately, Low-Value stimuli,
collapsing across Position conditions, then use a paired-samples t-test to test whether the Low-Value Ranks are higher. Table 5 shows
the results of these analyses; subsets where a statistically significant effect in the expected direction occurred are in bold. We see there
is evidence of an anchoring effect in both the Price and Temperature stimulus domains, but there is no evidence of an effect using
probabilities. We also see that whether the calibration data was collected before or concurrently with the experimental data had no
impact on whether there was an effect.
    Our overall results are also consistent across alternative analytic approaches. A parametric version of our Rank variable calculates
the z-score of experimental estimates relative to the calibration distribution (z = x− s m, where x is the experimental estimate, and m and s
are, respectively, the mean and standard deviation of the calibration estimates, including this experimental estimate). This z-score
across all studies was (non-significantly) negative for High-Value stimuli (M = -0.04, SD = 0.95; one-sample t-test [H0: μ = 0]: t[2286]
= 1.310, p = 0.190, d = 0.03 [− 0.01, 0.07]), and positive for Low-Value stimuli (M = 0.24, SD = 1.12; one-sample t-test [H0: μ = 0]: t
[2286] = 9.815, p < 0.001, d = 0.21 [0.16, 0.25]). A paired-samples t-test confirmed that z-scores were lower for High-Value stimuli
than Low-Value stimuli, indicating an anchoring effect, t(1352) = 7.675, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.21 [0.15, 0.26].
    We can also avoid transforming the estimates entirely, and conduct a mixed-effects regression, using the function mixed() from the
R package {afex} (Singmann et al., 2022), on both the calibration and experimental estimates. We use the ‘Type’ of estimate (cali­
bration or experimental) and Value as interacting fixed effects, with ‘Low’ set as the baseline Value level, and include a random
intercept for stimulus: (Estimate ~ Value*Type + (1|Stimulus)).8 If anchoring occurs, there should be a Value x Type interaction,
where experimental estimates are higher than calibration estimates for Low-Value stimuli, but lower for High-Value stimuli (Studies 9
and 10 could not be included in this analysis as the critical stimuli were neither high nor low value in the calibration study – they were
Anchoring-by-items, where there is no numeric anchor on a specified scale, is not therefore a natural prediction of Scale Distortion
theory. Similarly, Numeric Priming (Wong & Kwong, 2000) and Tversky and Kahneman’s (1974) original Anchoring-and-
Underadjustment heuristic also proceed from the assumption that anchors are numeric.
    We consistently observed that Low-Value stimuli were more strongly anchored upwards by High-Value stimuli, than High-Value
stimuli were anchored downwards by Low-Value stimuli. This was contrary to our expectation that the degree of anchoring would
depend upon an item’s variability. For judgments of the prices of products, we expected High-Value items would be anchored
downwards more than Low-Value items would be anchored upwards, because they are more variable, but we observed the opposite.
The same was true for judgments of probability stimuli. Although in the temperature domain, the countries with more variable
temperatures were anchored more, these were also the low-temperature countries, and so the parsimonious description of our result is
that Low-Value stimuli were anchored more than High-Value stimuli.
    Whilst the data were not consistent with our prediction that variability should moderate anchoring-by-item effects across domains,
we here outline a potential role of variability that future researchers may seek to test. Specifically, when considering the role of
variability in the Price domain, we neglected to consider skew in the distribution of stimulus values, but skew may be important − the
price of a product is positively skewed as prices can essentially be increased without limit by making exclusive or luxury variants of the
product. For example, adding diamonds to any product will increase its value. This ‘Diamond effect’ does not, however, work in reverse
– products cannot be cheapened without limit. This means it will often be more plausible for a Low-Value product to possess an
uncharacteristically high price (e.g., a comb, coated in diamonds and once owned by Queen Victoria) than for a High-Value product to
have an uncharacteristically low one. If people do make judgments as predicted by Selective Accessibility, the ‘Diamond effect’ may
suggest that people would tend to retrieve information consistent with two products having the same price by thinking of (more
plausible) expensive variants of the low-price item, rather than (less plausible) cheap versions of the high-price item.
    Ironically, Harris and Speekenbrink (2016)’s original claim that Mochon and Frederick’s (2013) null anchoring-by-items results
were consistent with High-Value items being anchored more than Low-Value items is contrary to the hypothesised ‘Diamond Effect’. A
post hoc explanation of Mochon and Frederick’s results can still, however, be advanced in terms of variability. Mochon and Frederick
specified a “Four pack of Duracell AA batteries” as the low anchor, which participants would most likely be familiar with as a standard
brand of batteries with very little price variability. Conversely, a “Canon Powershot camera” was likely less familiar to participants and
could plausibly therefore be a very cheap disposable camera or an expensive digital camera. Consequently, a hypothesis-consistent
search strategy would seem to necessitate a consideration of cheaper cameras, since it is simply not possible for a “Four pack of
Duracell AA batteries” to cost as much as an average camera.
    Ultimately, our use of value as a proxy for variability limits our understanding of the role of variability (and value) in anchoring-by-
items. Our post hoc explanations above are based on the contention that the shape of the price distributions for low and high value
stimuli also differed, in addition to their variability. Future studies should seek to disassociate and clarify the roles of value and
variability in anchoring-by-items effects, including consideration of all properties of judgment distributions (e.g., mean, skewness,
kurtosis, range), as well as the potential for different sources of variability exerting an influence (see e.g., Walters et al., 2023, for
examples of how different perceived sources of uncertainty can affect judgment and decision making). The relevance of this distri­
butional information will be maximised where it is collected within individuals, as it is the plausibility of different values to an in­
dividual that we contend (see also Mussweiler & Strack, 2000a; Turner & Schley, 2016) should ultimately predict the size of anchoring-
by-items effects.
    The observed anchoring-by-items effect across our studies was small, with a meta-analytic Hedge’s g of 0.25. This is much smaller
than the large meta-analytic effect size estimated by Schley and Weingarten (2025) for numerical anchoring effects, d = 0.88.12 This
makes sense – item anchors have uncertain values, and so should induce weaker anchoring effects (Turner & Schley, 2016). In addition,
estimates of both stimuli (anchor and target) are anchored, such that there are really two effects operating in each instance. Future
studies into anchoring should bear this small effect size in mind, as individual studies will require large samples to be confident of
finding effects for such effect sizes – 95% power requires N = 210 for a paired-samples t-test, and N = 834 for an independent-samples
t-test.13
    The small effect size is a likely reason why three previously published studies, and five of our own, individually reported null results
for anchoring-by-items. All but one of these studies observed numerical trends in the expected direction (the current Study 9 being the
only exception), but may have been underpowered for their inferential tests. Mochon and Frederick’s (2013) Experiment 1, for
example, only has 11% power to find an effect size of g = 0.25.14 Additionally, future studies should ensure that the (unanchored)
estimates of the items to be used as high and low anchors have demonstrably different values – neither Chapman and Johnson (1994),
nor Bahník et al. (2019) reported data on participants’ perceived values of their anchor items in a control condition, and it is not
obvious that participants would have perceived their values to be substantially different in every case. Following Jacowitz and
Kahneman’s (1994) prescription that the values of anchors should fall beyond the upper or lower 15th percentile of the target
stimulus’s value distribution, as we were able to do here (taking the value of the anchor to be the median calibration estimate), may be
a useful rule to follow. Relatedly, it is noteworthy that the largest observed effect size in our studies was Study 1, where the median
calibration estimates of the low and high-value stimuli differed by factors of between 44 and 500 – where the largest difference across
the other studies was a factor of 25 (Study 6). This aligns with previous research finding that anchors which are more ‘extreme’ (lying

further from the typical value of the estimand) produce stronger anchoring effects (e.g., Lieder et al., 2018a, 2018b).
    In our analyses of ‘notable subsets’ of studies, we observed a significant anchoring-by-items effect for Prices and Temperatures as
stimuli, but not for Probabilities. We think it is premature to conclude that this indicates a true difference across stimulus domains,
predominantly because of the small effect size we are dealing with here. We were interested in using probability stimuli because the
probability scale is definitively bounded at both ends, unlike prices, which are bounded at 0. We had considered that this asymmetrical
bounding could contribute to why we saw that price estimates could be anchored upwards more easily than downward, as it asym­
metrically influences potential range and skewness. Does the null aggregate result in the Probability studies therefore suggest that the
anchoring-by-items effect relies upon asymmetrical bounds? We see no theoretical reason why this should be the case, but ultimately
leave this as a question for future research.
    Studies 9 and 10 employed a different design from Studies 1–8. They were originally designed to provide a straightforward test of
an anchoring-by-items effect (asking the question “Are estimates for the medium stimulus higher when compared with a high stimulus
than when compared with a low stimulus?” – see Supplementary Material 5), and were only subsequently included in the overall meta-
analysis. Is the failure to observe anchoring effects in the ‘straightforward test’ indicative of a peculiar characteristic of Studies 1–8 that
makes an anchoring effect more likely to be observed there? We argue that the answer is “no”, for the following reasons. Firstly, from a
psychological perspective, an individual participant’s experience is identical across the two designs. In all studies reported in this
manuscript, participants see a higher value item compared with a lower value item before making a judgment about one of those items.
Secondly, the analyses of low and high-value items across our ten studies already demonstrate that anchoring should be observed in an
appropriately powered ‘straightforward test’. This is because, overall, low-value items were reliably anchored relative to a no-anchor
control (calibration estimates); there was also evidence (though less robust) that high-value items were anchored relative to a no-
anchor control.15 To demonstrate that anchoring could be observed in a ‘straightforward test’, we could design a study in which
we compare estimates of a calculator after comparison with a second-hand car (high anchor) and a single onion (low anchor). Such a
study, however, seems unnecessary given the results of Study 1. Given that comparison with the high-value items (including a car)
anchored estimates of the low-value items (including a calculator) relative to the control condition, as long as comparison with an
onion does not increase estimates of the calculator, an anchoring effect would be observed in a comparison of estimates following the
high anchor (car) and the low anchor (onion), given sufficient statistical power. Thirdly, one might speculate that somehow the
ranking procedure, which is not employed in Studies 9 and 10, artificially produces (or exaggerates) anchoring effects, despite this
approach closely mirroring that proposed in Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995). This is demonstrably not the case, as illustrated by the
fact that our findings were corroborated by an alternative z-scored based analysis and in a mixed-effects regression analysis using
untransformed data. Rather, we propose that the apparent difference in observed effects between the two designs is most likely an
artifact of the small effect we are dealing with (Studies 2, 3 & 7 all individually did not show a significant effect as well).
    We have thus far argued that there is no specific design choice that differentiates those studies that have observed a significant
anchoring effect, and those that have not. We have highlighted the need for more research to understand the influence of value,

anchoring bias is larger the more uncertain people are about the quantity to be

people knowledgeable about the quantity to be estimated were immune to the anchoring
bias whereas less knowledgeable people were susceptible to it. While familiarity (Wright

expertise appears to at least reduce it (Northcraft & Neale, 1987). Other experiments
have systematically varied the distance from the anchor to the correct value. Their
results suggested that the magnitude of the anchoring bias initially increases with the
distance from the anchor to the correct value (Russo & Schoemaker, 1989). Yet this
linear increase of the anchoring bias does not continue indefinitely. Chapman and

the anchoring bias less than increasing a realistic anchor by the same amount.

Resource-rational anchoring-and-adjustment provides a theoretical explanation
for insufficient adjustment from provided and self-generated anchors in terms of a
rational speed-accuracy tradeoff, but how accurately does this describe empirical data?
To answer this question, we fit our model to two well-known anchoring experiments:
one with provided and one with self-generated anchors.
 A RATIONAL PERSPECTIVE ON ANCHORING-AND-ADJUSTMENT                                         25


       Provided anchors. As an example of adjustment from provided anchors, we
chose the study by Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995), because it rigorously quantifies the
anchoring bias. Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) asked their participants two questions
about each of several unknown quantities: First they asked whether the quantity is
larger or smaller than a certain value–the provided anchor. Next they asked the
participant to estimate that quantity. For the first half of the participants the anchor
was a low value (i.e. the 15th percentile of estimates people make when no anchor is
provided), and for the second half of the participants the anchor was a high value (i.e.
the 85th percentile). People’s estimates were significantly higher when the anchor was
high than when it was low. Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) quantified this effect by the
anchoring index (AI), which is the percentage of the distance from the low to the high
anchor that is retained in people’s estimates:

                        Median(X̂high anchor ) − Median(X̂low anchor )
                 AI =                                                  · 100%             (5)
                               high anchor − low anchor

Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) found that the average anchoring index was about 50%.
This means that the difference between people’s estimates in the high versus the low
anchor condition retained about half of the distance between the two anchors.
       We determined the uncertainty σ for each of the 15 quantities by the elicitation
method described above. Since Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) measured people’s
median estimates in the absence of any anchor, we used those values as our estimates of
the expected values µ, because their sample and its median estimates were significantly
different from ours.
       Next, we estimated the adjustment step-size parameter and the relative time
cost parameter by minimizing the sum of squared errors between the predicted and the
observed anchoring indices. According to the estimated parameters, people performed
29 adjustments with an average step-size of 22.4 units. With these two estimated
parameters the model accurately captures the insufficient adjustment from provided
anchors reported by Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995): The model’s adjustments are
insufficient (i.e. anchoring index > 0; see Equation 5) on all questions for which this
had been observed empirically but not for the question on which it had not been
 A RATIONAL PERSPECTIVE ON ANCHORING-AND-ADJUSTMENT                                     26


observed; see Figure 7. Our model also captured the magnitude of the anchoring bias:
the model’s average anchoring index of 53.22% was very close to its empirical
counterpart of 48.48%. Furthermore, our model also captured for which questions the
anchoring bias was high and for which it was low: the correlation between the predicted
and the empirical anchoring indices (r(13) = 0.62, p = 0.0135). The simulated and
empirical anchoring effects are shown in Figure 7.
